description: My team consists of me and a colleague of mine officially. I have won a certificate in Astrophysics and another in Quantum Mechanics. I study not out of necessity but out of love for this thing we call science. I believe the language our universe speaks in is mathematics, I have another unofficial friend who majors in astrophysics. Please join this team if you love science for its beauty and not its money.
summary:
Lycoris, is a result of immense hard work from me and my teammates. It first started as a simple question of how much O2 would be required to traverse a distance on Mars, nothing else was considered. But throughout the journey I developed 4 versions (Omega, Alpha, Gamma, Gluon) and then finalized it with Version : Claire. 
What is Lycoris?
It plans a route around steep ground on a 20 m/pixel elevation model
It calculates times, O2/person, Radiation dosage, daylight. Each with a range.
Craters are calculated by both : Going across it, and taking a detour around it
A helmet HUD Walk has been designed to simulate an actual walk with animations and clearly defined calculations
Every number when interacted with, opens its calculations.
Experimental Claire is most likely, the strongest part of my project. I, when working on Version Gluon, noticed a strange pattern regarding temperature and radiation ON MARS only. Theres an entire experimental Claire mode which switches calculations to a hypothesis.
Future crew will need plans they can check, verify, and thus trust.
details:
What it does

  • Mission map:
    • You pick a start and a destination at Jezero.
    • Lycoris plans a route on the USGS CTX elevation model, avoiding slopes above 20° and treating 30° as no-go on foot.
    • It reports distance, time, oxygen per crew member, radiation dose and daylight.
    • The route assessment can only say NO-GO, UNDETERMINED or WITHIN ENTERED LIMITS. Any failed check gives NO-GO, and any missing check gives UNDETERMINED.
  • Crater ahead: Belva is my test case: 920 m across, 68 m deep, with 21° walls. Crossing it is 1,045 m, about 37 min and 42.0 L of oxygen per person. Going around is 1,602 m, about 38.5 min and 40.7 L. The shorter path isn’t automatically the cheaper one.
  • Helmet HUD: replays the planned walk with oxygen, dose so far, next waypoint, sunset and estimated crew vitals. The vitals are estimates, not telemetry.
  • Calculation records: every number opens its formula, inputs, units, sources and assumptions. An AI guide can explain a record. If the AI is unavailable, the worked calculation is still there.
  • Experimental Claire: a separate section behind the warning “The radiation estimates may be wrong.” It shows the standard dose model and a temperature-adjusted one side by side. Their difference is a difference between two models, not measured exposure.
  • Data sources page: lists every map layer and every engine setting, labelled MEASURED, ASSUMED, MODEL or NOT MODELLED.

How it works

  • Radiation:
    • Uses Dose(P) = D_ref · exp[−μ(P − P_ref)/37.1], with the air overhead taken as pressure divided by Mars gravity.
    • I fitted it to 142 sols of Curiosity RAD dose and REMS pressure data (2012–14).
    • Within a sol, dose falls as pressure rises. My fitted μ is 0.009–0.017 cm²/g, below the 0.022 I first assumed from Guo et al. (2015).
    • I scale it from Gale to Jezero using the pressure difference from the Mars Climate Database. That’s a model transfer, not a measurement at Jezero.
  • Climate: Mars Climate Database v6.2 pressure and temperature by season and hour. In the seasons I tested, its pressure matched Curiosity REMS within 0.4–1.3% at Gale. That’s encouraging, but it doesn’t validate every hour or Jezero itself.
    • Uses NASA Johnson Space Center suit-mass figures: 82 kg crew member, 104 kg suit plus 23 kg carried, VO₂max 36 ml/kg/min.
    • Walking cost uses the ACSM walking equation adjusted for Mars gravity, plus fatigue and rest rules.
    • These are model assumptions, not a calibrated pressure-suit model.
  • Season and daylight: solar longitude from Allison & McEwen (2000).
  • Built with: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules hosted on Cloudflare, PowerShell scripts for the PDS and MCD data, and JPL Mars Trek basemaps.

What I considered

  • The first version of this project had real mistakes:
    • an oxygen formula that only worked for one minute;
    • a crater formula that multiplied a 3D shape by oxygen;
    • a theory that colder air directly means less radiation.
  • I kept the corrections visible instead of hiding them.
  • The temperature question is still open. Temperature and pressure move together within a sol (correlation −0.80), so my data can’t yet say which one matters. Claire keeps that question visible without letting it decide anything.
  • I also don’t model water, battery, CO₂ scrubbing, heat storage or solar storms yet. Those show as “Not modelled” rather than being filled in.

Known limits and next steps

  • Rover mode isn’t implemented yet.
  • The crater comparison uses an idealised bowl.
  • Claire’s held-out validation hasn’t been run.
  • Next, I want to compare the climate model against Perseverance MEDA pressure at Jezero, and test the temperature hypothesis on sols I didn’t use to fit it.
    Use of Super Intelligence
    I used Claude (Anthropic) as a research and coding assistant:
  • verification of calculations, helping in derivation of multiple formulae and discovery of them, insight on science
  • for processing approximately 8,172 Curiosity readings across 142 sols, plus the Mars Climate Database;
  • for helping in assmebling the demo video. (Approximately 35% was done by claude for cleaning up the fonts)
  • for converting 400+ dense notes of research into a simple draft (this text was summarized by claude based on my research notes)

The research questions, hypotheses and design decisions are mine.
